identification.summary: Antique Typhoon (formerly tracked as Storm-0558) is a China-based threat actor that Microsoft says has espionage objectives and mainly seeks unauthorized access to employee email accounts at targeted organizations [S1][S8]. In 2023 it used an acquired Microsoft account (MSA) consumer signing key to forge authentication tokens and read Exchange Online and Outlook.com email at about 25 organizations, including government agencies [S1]. The US Cyber Safety Review Board (CSRB) later found the intrusion was preventable and resulted from 'a cascade of security failures at Microsoft' [S6][S7].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: interest in OAuth applications, token theft and token replay since at least August 2021 [S1]. Forged-token email access began 2023-05-15 [S1]. CSRB Acting Deputy Chair Dmitri Alperovitch said industry has tracked the actor for over two decades (reporting) [S6].
identification.notes: Microsoft renamed Storm-0558 to Antique Typhoon in an August 2024 update to its July 2023 analysis [S1]; Microsoft's naming map lists Storm-0558 as the other name [S8]. Microsoft reports minor overlaps with Violet Typhoon (ZIRCONIUM, APT31) but holds high confidence that this is a distinct group [S1]. No MITRE ATT&CK group ID was found.

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (assessed). Microsoft calls the actor China-based with espionage objectives [S1]. Press coverage of the CSRB report describes the group as affiliated with the PRC; China has denied involvement [S5][S6].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft assesses with moderate confidence that the actor is China-based, and with high confidence that it is distinct from Violet Typhoon [S1]. The CSRB report characterizes the actor as PRC-affiliated (per press coverage; the report text was not opened) [S6]. No indictment or sanctions naming this actor were found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and incident response, including activity hours matching China Standard Time, Monday to Friday [S1]; CSRB review of the 2023 intrusion (via press coverage) [S6][S7].

objectives: Espionage through collection of email from government, diplomatic, economic and legislative targets, with particular focus on US and European bodies and on individuals tied to Taiwan and Uyghur geopolitical interests [S1]. In the 2023 campaign, nine of ten compromised State Department accounts reportedly belonged to people working on East Asia and the Pacific [S5].

sectors: Individuals tied to Taiwan and Uyghur interests [S1]
targeting.notes: The 2023 campaign hit about 25 organizations per Microsoft [S1]; CSRB coverage cites 22 organizations and over 500 individuals, including Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo, US Ambassador to China R. Nicholas Burns and Congressman Don Bacon [S7]. About 60,000 unclassified emails were taken from 10 State Department accounts, along with a list of the department's email accounts (reporting a Senate briefing and State Department confirmation) [S5].

capabilities.summary: Cloud identity abuse is the signature capability. The actor forged Azure AD and MSA tokens with an acquired MSA consumer signing key, which Microsoft code accepted for enterprise tokens because of a validation error, and abused a flaw in the GetAccessTokenForResource API to mint new tokens from issued ones [S1]. It ran a custom web panel for token replay, used dedicated SoftEther proxy infrastructure, and used PowerShell and Python scripts with hardcoded bearer tokens to call the OWA Exchange Store REST service, optionally over Tor or SOCKS5 [S1]. Wiz assessed the key could have signed OpenID v2.0 tokens for other Azure AD applications such as SharePoint, Teams and OneDrive, though no exploitation of those services was confirmed [S3][S9]. Historically Microsoft has seen phishing, credential harvesting, exploitation of public-facing applications leading to China Chopper web shells, the Cigril malware launched via DLL search-order hijacking, and credential theft from LSASS memory and the SAM hive [S1]. Microsoft's September 2023 account of key theft (crash dump moved to a corporate debugging environment, then a compromised engineer account) was later revised: in March 2024 Microsoft said it had not found a crash dump containing the key [S2].

campaigns.name: Early OAuth and token-theft interest
campaigns.summary: Microsoft says the actor has shown interest in OAuth applications, token theft and token replay since at least August 2021 [S1].

campaigns.name: Exchange Online / Outlook.com forged-token intrusion
campaigns.summary: Using forged tokens signed with an acquired MSA consumer key, the actor accessed email at about 25 organizations, including government agencies [S1]. A federal agency detected anomalous MailItemsAccessed events and reported them; Microsoft began its investigation on 2023-06-16 and blocked the key [S1][S4]. About 60,000 State Department emails were stolen [S5].

campaigns.name: CISA/FBI advisory AA23-193A
campaigns.summary: CISA and the FBI released advisory AA23-193A on detecting the activity through enhanced logging, including MailItemsAccessed [S4].

campaigns.name: Microsoft key-acquisition findings
campaigns.summary: Microsoft published its most probable explanation of how the key was obtained, then revised it on 2024-03-12 after finding no crash dump containing the key [S2].

campaigns.name: CSRB review published
campaigns.summary: The CSRB concluded the intrusion was preventable and faulted Microsoft's security culture; it recommended security reforms by Microsoft and other cloud providers (reporting) [S6][S7].

campaigns.name: Rename to Antique Typhoon
campaigns.summary: Microsoft updated its analysis to track Storm-0558 as Antique Typhoon [S1].

diamond.adversary: China-based espionage actor (Microsoft, moderate confidence), active on China Standard Time working hours [S1]; described as PRC-affiliated in CSRB coverage [S6].
diamond.capability: Forged MSA/Azure AD tokens, token replay panel, PowerShell and Python OWA scripts, China Chopper web shells, Cigril malware, credential dumping [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Dedicated token-replay servers with a web panel at /#/login, SoftEther proxy hosts fingerprinted by JARM, Tor and SOCKS5 routing [S1].
diamond.victim: About 25 organizations incl. US government agencies and associated consumer accounts [S1]; State Department, Commerce Secretary and other officials [S5][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on US and European diplomacy and East Asia policy, plus Taiwan- and Uyghur-related individuals [S1][S5].
diamond.technology: Microsoft cloud identity: MSA consumer signing keys, Azure AD token validation, Exchange Online/OWA, Outlook.com [S1][S3].

gaps: How the actor actually obtained the MSA signing key is unresolved; Microsoft withdrew its crash-dump explanation in March 2024 [S2].
CSRB report (cisa.gov PDF) and CISA advisory AA23-193A could not be opened; details are from press coverage and search summaries [S4][S6][S7].
Victim count differs: Microsoft about 25 organizations vs CSRB coverage 22 organizations and over 500 individuals [S1][S7].

The reported link to Operation Aurora (2009) and RSA SecurID (2011) comes from a CSRB official's quoted remark in press coverage, not a verified primary attribution; vendor cluster boundaries for those older intrusions are not established here [S6].
Microsoft's July 11, 2023 blog and MSRC posts on blogs.microsoft.com and msrc.microsoft.com, and Wiz's original post, could not be fetched.
No public reporting on Antique Typhoon activity after 2023 was found; current operations are unknown.
Whether the key was used against Azure AD applications beyond Exchange Online (Wiz scenario) is unconfirmed [S3][S9].
No MITRE ATT&CK group entry was found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The operational environment includes commercial cloud identity providers and hosted email (Exchange Online/M365). Key terrain sits in the provider's token-signing infrastructure, outside DoD control [S1][S3]. STEP 2: A provider-side key compromise lets the actor bypass tenant authentication and MFA entirely, so tenant hardening alone does not close the gap. Detection depends on audit logs such as MailItemsAccessed [S1][S4]. STEP 3: Doctrinal template: acquire signing material or credentials, forge or replay tokens through dedicated proxy infrastructure, then run scripted bulk mailbox collection of selected officials, with no on-host malware in the victim tenant [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet, targeted email collection against officials working East Asia and Pacific policy, especially around diplomatic events [S1][S5]. MDCOA is undetected forged-token access to DoD or coalition M365 tenants during a Taiwan crisis, exposing planning traffic and enabling follow-on targeting [S1][S3]. Candidate indicators: MailItemsAccessed from unusual AppIDs, tokens with unexpected issuers or key IDs, mailbox access from SoftEther/JARM-fingerprinted or Tor egress, and REST calls to OWA from unknown clients [S1][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: the intrusion was found by a customer agency's logs, not the provider, so JCC2 views must ingest cloud audit telemetry (premium logging) from mission-relevant tenants [S1][S4][S7]. (2) Authorities: response to a cloud-provider-side compromise relies on the provider and on CISA/FBI channels; define in advance who requests provider forensics and log access [S4][S7]. (3) Mission assurance: treat unclassified commercial email as exposed to collection for East Asia operations and keep sensitive planning on DoD-controlled systems [S5]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with CISA, the FBI and cloud providers quickly, as AA23-193A did; plan for vendor root-cause findings to change over time [S2][S4].
